big.note: Romance 'big' (grande, grand, grande, grande) all come from Latin 'grandis' — root of 'grand', 'grandeur'. Latin's other word, 'magnus' (root of 'magnify', 'magnitude'), survives in scientific vocabulary. English 'big' / German 'groß' are Germanic.

bird.note: Spanish 'pájaro' and Portuguese 'pássaro' come from Latin 'passer' (sparrow). Italian 'uccello' and French 'oiseau' come from Latin 'avicellus', a diminutive of 'avis' (root of 'aviary', 'aviation'). English 'bird' and German 'Vogel' are Germanic.

black.note: Spanish 'negro', French 'noir', Italian 'nero' all come from Latin 'niger' — root of 'denigrate'. Portuguese commonly uses 'preto' (from Latin 'apprehensus', pressed-tight/dense). English 'black' and German 'schwarz' are Germanic.

blue.note: Two families here: Spanish/Portuguese 'azul' is from Arabic 'lāzaward' (lapis lazuli), while French 'bleu', Italian 'blu', English 'blue', German 'blau' all share the Germanic root *blēwaz. Latin had no single common word; 'caeruleus' (sky-blue) is the classical term.

book.note: Romance 'book' (libro, livre, libro, livro) all come from Latin 'liber' — root of 'library' and 'libretto'. English 'book' and German 'Buch' come from the Germanic word for beech wood, on which early runes were carved.

bread.note: Romance 'bread' (pan, pain, pane, pão) all come from Latin 'panis' — the root of 'pantry', 'companion' (one you share bread with), and 'empanada'. English 'bread' and German 'Brot' are Germanic.

cat.note: Almost every European 'cat' (gato, chat, gatto, gato, Katze, cat) descends from Late Latin 'cattus'. This word spread across the whole continent with the domestic cat itself — one of the most uniform cognates in the deck.

child.note: French 'enfant' and English 'infant' both come from Latin 'infans' (literally 'not speaking'). Portuguese 'criança' is from Latin 'creare' (to create — cf. 'creature'). Spanish 'niño' and Italian 'bambino' are nursery words. German 'Kind' (cf. 'kin', 'kindergarten') is Germanic.

cold.note: Romance 'cold' (frío, froid, freddo, frio) all come from Latin 'frigidus' — the root of 'frigid', 'refrigerator'. English 'cold' and German 'kalt' are Germanic — and interestingly share a root with Latin 'gelidus' (gel/cold).

day.note: Spanish/Portuguese 'día/dia' come straight from Latin 'dies'. French 'jour' and Italian 'giorno' took a different Latin path through 'diurnum' (daily) — the root of 'journal' and 'journey'. English 'day' / German 'Tag' are Germanic.

dog.note: French 'chien', Italian 'cane', and Portuguese 'cão' come from Latin 'canis' (root of 'canine'). Spanish broke ranks with 'perro' (uncertain origin). English 'dog' and German 'Hund' (cf. 'hound') are Germanic.

example.it: La terra è la nostra casa.

earth.note: Romance 'earth' (tierra, terre, terra, terra) all come from Latin 'terra' — root of 'territory', 'terrain', 'terrestrial'. English 'earth' and German 'Erde' are the Germanic pair.

example.es: La caja está vacía, el vaso vacío.
example.it: La scatola è vuota, il vaso vuoto.

eye.note: Romance 'eye' (ojo, œil, occhio, olho) all come from Latin 'oculus' — root of 'ocular', 'binoculars', 'inoculate'. English 'eye' and German 'Auge' descend from the parallel root *h₃ókʷs.

father.note: Latin 'pater' (root of 'paternal', 'patriarch') gives padre/père/padre/pai. English 'father' and German 'Vater' come from the same *ph₂tḗr — the Latin 'p' became Germanic 'f' by Grimm's Law.

fire.note: Romance 'fire' (fuego, feu, fuoco, fogo) come from Latin 'focus' (hearth — yes, the same word as English 'focus'). Latin's poetic word was 'ignis' (root of 'ignite'). English 'fire' and German 'Feuer' descend from a separate root *péh₂wr̥.

example.en: The fish is in the water.
example.es: El pez está en el agua.

fish.note: Romance 'fish' (pez, poisson, pesce, peixe) all come from Latin 'piscis' — root of 'Pisces', 'piscine'. English 'fish' and German 'Fisch' are the Germanic reflex of the same root (Latin 'p' → Germanic 'f').

five.note: Latin 'quinque' → 'cinco/cinq/cinque'; English 'five' and German 'fünf' show the Germanic 'f' for the same root *pénkʷe (think 'penta-' in Greek loanwords).

flower.note: Romance 'flower' (flor, fleur, fiore, flor) and English 'flower' all come from Latin 'flos' (stem 'flor-') — root of 'floral', 'flora', 'flourish'. German 'Blume' is Germanic (cf. English 'bloom' and 'blossom').

foot.note: Romance 'foot' (pie, pied, piede, pé) all come from Latin 'pes' (stem 'ped-') — root of 'pedal', 'pedestrian', 'pedestal'. English 'foot' and German 'Fuß' descend from the same *pṓds, with Latin 'p' → Germanic 'f'.

four.note: Romance 'qu-' forms (cuatro, quatre, quattro, quatro) all come from Latin 'quattuor'; English 'four' and German 'vier' kept the 'f/v' Germanic reflex of the same *kʷetwóres.

friend.note: Romance 'friend' (amigo, ami, amico) is from Latin 'amicus', built on 'amare' (to love) — the same root as 'amiable' and 'amity'. English 'friend' and German 'Freund' are Germanic.

good.note: Romance 'good' (bueno, bon, buono, bom) all come from Latin 'bonus' — the root of 'bonus', 'bonafide', 'benefit'. English 'good' and German 'gut' are an unrelated Germanic pair.

green.note: Romance 'green' (verde, vert, verde, verde) all come from Latin 'viridis' — root of 'verdant', 'verdure'. English 'green' and German 'grün' share a Germanic root with 'grow' and 'grass'.

hand.note: Romance 'hand' (mano, main, mano, mão) all come from Latin 'manus' — the root of 'manual', 'manage', 'manuscript'. Note 'mano' is feminine even though it ends in '-o'. English/German 'hand' is the Germanic word.

head.note: Spanish 'cabeza' and Portuguese 'cabeça' come from Latin 'capitia', from 'caput' (root of 'capital', 'captain', 'decapitate'). French 'tête' and Italian 'testa' come from Latin 'testa' (a pot — slang for the head). English 'head' and German 'Kopf' (originally 'cup') are Germanic.

heart.note: Romance 'heart' (corazón, cœur, cuore, coração) all come from Latin 'cor' (stem 'cord-') — root of 'cordial', 'courage', 'record'. English 'heart' and German 'Herz' descend from the same *ḱḗr — once you spot the 'c/h' + 'r' you see them all.

horse.note: Romance 'horse' (caballo, cheval, cavallo, cavalo) come from Latin 'caballus' (workhorse, nag) — root of 'cavalry', 'chivalry', 'cavalier'. Classical Latin 'equus' (root of 'equestrian') lost out. English 'horse' and German 'Pferd' are Germanic.

hot.note: Romance 'hot' (caliente, chaud, caldo, quente) all come from Latin 'calidus' — the root of 'calorie', 'cauldron', 'nonchalant'. The 'cal-/chal-' is the heat. English 'hot' and German 'heiß' are Germanic.

house.note: Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese keep Latin 'casa' (cottage) unchanged. French chose 'maison' (from Latin 'mansio', a dwelling — root of 'mansion'). English 'house' and German 'Haus' are Germanic twins.

light.note: Romance 'light' (luz, lumière, luce, luz) all come from Latin 'lux' (stem 'luc-') — root of 'lucid', 'translucent', 'Lucifer' (light-bearer). The same root *lewk- also gives English 'light' and German 'Licht'. A canon-tier word: light ties to the physics branch.

example.fr: La route est longue, le chemin long.
example.it: La strada è lunga, il cammino lungo.

love.note: Romance 'love' (amor, amour, amore, amor) all come from Latin 'amor' — root of 'amorous', 'enamored', 'paramour'. English 'love' and German 'Liebe' are Germanic, from *lewbʰ- (the same root that gives Latin 'libido').

man.note: Romance 'man' (hombre, homme, uomo, homem) all come from Latin 'homo' (human being) — root of 'human', 'homage', 'Homo sapiens'. The silent Spanish/Portuguese 'h-' is the old Latin 'h'. English 'man' and German 'Mann' are Germanic.

example.en: I drink milk in the morning.

milk.note: Romance 'milk' (leche, lait, latte, leite) all come from Latin 'lac' (stem 'lact-') — root of 'lactose', 'lactic', 'latte'. English 'milk' and German 'Milch' are Germanic, though distantly related via *gʷálakts.

example.es: La luna está llena esta noche.

moon.note: Romance 'moon' (luna, lune, luna, lua) all come from Latin 'luna' (root of 'lunar', 'lunatic'). English 'moon' and German 'Mond' descend from a different root *mḗh₁n̥s — also the source of 'month'.

mother.note: One of the oldest cognates in the family: Latin 'mater' (root of 'maternal', 'matrix') gives madre/mère/madre/mãe, and the same *méh₂tēr gives English 'mother' and German 'Mutter'. Every form starts with 'm-'.

name.note: A near-universal cognate: Latin 'nomen' (root of 'nominate', 'noun', 'nominal') gives nombre/nom/nome/nome, and the same *h₁nómn̥ gives English 'name' and German 'Name'. They all keep 'n-...-m'.

new.note: A clean cognate: Latin 'novus' (root of 'novel', 'innovate', 'renovate') gives nuevo/nouveau/nuovo/novo, and the same *néwos gives English 'new' and German 'neu'. Every form keeps 'n-' + a 'v/w'.

night.note: A beautiful cognate set: Latin 'nox' (stem 'noct-', as in 'nocturnal') gives noche/nuit/notte/noite, and the same root *nókʷts gives English 'night' and German 'Nacht'. Every form keeps the 'n-' and a 't/ch'.

example.it: Il sette è il mio numero.

number.note: Romance 'number' (número, nombre, numero, número) and English 'number' all come from Latin 'numerus' — root of 'numeral', 'enumerate', 'numerous'. German 'Zahl' is Germanic (cf. 'tale', a count). A canon-tier word tying to the mathematics branch.

old.note: Romance 'old' (viejo, vieux, vecchio, velho) come from Latin 'vetulus' (little-old), a diminutive of 'vetus' — the root of 'veteran' and 'inveterate'. English 'old' and German 'alt' are Germanic.

one.note: Romance '1' all descend from Latin 'unus'; English 'one' and German 'eins' are the Germanic branch of the same Indo-European root *óynos.

red.note: Spanish 'rojo', French 'rouge', Italian 'rosso' come from Latin 'russus/ruber' — root of 'ruby', 'rubric'. The whole family, including English 'red' and German 'rot', traces to *h₁rewdʰ-. Portuguese went its own way with 'vermelho' (from 'vermiculus', the red dye-worm).

example.en: The shop is on the right.
example.es: La tienda está a la derecha.
La película es corta, el día corto.

small.note: The Romance words for 'small' are a scattered family (pequeño, petit, piccolo, pequeno) tied to an expressive 'pikk-/pitt-' root for 'little'. Latin used 'parvus'. English 'small' and German 'klein' are Germanic.

star.note: Romance 'star' (estrella, étoile, stella, estrela) all come from Latin 'stella' — root of 'stellar', 'constellation'. English 'star' and German 'Stern' descend from the same *h₂stḗr. A canon-tier word tying to the cosmology branch.

sun.note: Latin 'sol' (root of 'solar') is nearly untouched in Spanish/Portuguese 'sol' and Italian 'sole'; French 'soleil' adds a diminutive. English 'sun' and German 'Sonne' are the Germanic side of the same *sóh₂wl̥.

ten.note: Latin 'decem' (cf. 'decimal', 'December') → 'diez/dix/dieci/dez'; English 'ten' and German 'zehn' descend from the same *déḱm̥. The 'dec-' prefix you know from math is right here.

three.note: Latin 'tres' gives Spanish/Portuguese 'tres/três' directly; the English 'th' and German 'dr' both trace to the same *tréyes — once you see 'tri-' you see them all.

time.note: Romance 'time' (tiempo, temps, tempo, tempo) all come from Latin 'tempus' — root of 'temporary', 'tempo', 'contemporary'. (In Spanish/Italian/Portuguese it also means 'weather'.) English 'time' and German 'Zeit' are Germanic.

tree.note: Romance 'tree' (árbol, arbre, albero, árvore) all come from Latin 'arbor' — root of 'arbor', 'arboretum'. English 'tree' and German 'Baum' are Germanic (Baum is the source of English 'beam').

truth.note: Romance 'truth' (verdad, vérité, verità, verdade) all come from Latin 'veritas' — root of 'verify', 'verdict', 'very'. The '-dad/-té/-tà/-dade' endings all reflect Latin '-tas'. English 'truth' and German 'Wahrheit' are Germanic. A canon-tier word: truth underlies every branch.

two.note: Every form here comes from Indo-European *dwóh₁: Latin 'duo' → Romance, while English 'two' and German 'zwei' kept the Germanic shape (the 'd→t/z' shift is Grimm's Law).

water.note: All Romance forms descend from Latin 'aqua' (think 'aquarium', 'aquatic'); English 'water' is Germanic (cf. German 'Wasser'), from the parallel root *wódr̥.

white.note: Romance 'white' (blanco, blanc, bianco, branco) is borrowed from Germanic *blankaz (shining) — the same root as English 'blank'. Classical Latin used 'albus' (root of 'album', 'albino'). English 'white' / German 'weiß' are native Germanic.

wine.note: A perfect cognate: Latin 'vinum' (root of 'vine', 'vintage', 'vinegar') gives vino/vin/vino/vinho, and the borrowed-into-Germanic 'Wein' and 'wine' too. Every form keeps the 'v/w' + 'n'.

woman.note: Spanish 'mujer' and Portuguese 'mulher' come from Latin 'mulier'. French 'femme' comes from Latin 'femina' (root of 'feminine'). Italian 'donna' is from 'domina' (lady — root of 'Madonna', 'dame'). English 'woman' and German 'Frau' are Germanic.

word.note: Spanish 'palabra', Italian 'parola', Portuguese 'palavra' come from Latin 'parabola' (comparison — also the root of 'parable' and, via French, 'parole'). Latin 'verbum' (root of 'verb', 'verbal') links to English 'word' and German 'Wort'.

year.note: Romance 'year' (año, an, anno, ano) all come from Latin 'annus' — root of 'annual', 'anniversary'. Spanish 'ñ' is a squeezed double-n. English 'year' and German 'Jahr' are Germanic.

yellow.note: Spanish 'amarillo' and Portuguese 'amarelo' come from Latin 'amarellus' (bitterish). French 'jaune' and Italian 'giallo' come from Latin 'galbinus' (greenish-yellow). English 'yellow' and German 'gelb' share a Germanic root with 'gold' and 'glow'.
